objects: sample correlation matrix; sample size n; variable count p
conclusion: The sample correlation matrix can perform poorly when the number of variables is large relative to the number of samples, motivating shrinkage or regularization.
scope: Motivation for adaptive correlation shrinkage with missing data.
span: Estimating the correlation matrix of a set of variables is a fundamental problem in statistics. The simplest estimator, the sample correlation matrix, can perform poorly when the number of variables (p) is large compared with the number of samples (n). This problem has motivated many alternative estimators, most of them based on shrinkage or regularization methods.

span: The rationale for the more restrictive unimodal choices (U, SU, U+ , SN ) is that they ensure shrinkage towards a common point, and also regularize the estimate of g compared with a fully non-parametric approach. Stephens [2016] focused on the case where the mode of g was at 0, but the ashr package also implements methods to estimate the location of the mode, which may also be useful in this context. Results in this paper were generated using G = U with mode at 0 unless otherwise stated.

objects: standard deviation sij; nonnormal pairs; bootstrap standard errors
assumptions: variables are not pairwise normally distributed
conclusion: The stated analytic standard-deviation formula fails without pairwise normality; the authors suggest robust data transformations or bootstrap standard errors.
scope: Alternatives are suggested rather than a new distribution-free calibration theorem.
span: If the variables are not pairwise normally distributed, then the representation of sij as in Equation (4) does not hold. One approach in this context is to use transformations of the data that are more robust to the non-normality of the data, for example - Box-cox, ranks, rank-based inverse normal (RIN) transformations [Bishara and Hittner, 2015, 2017]. Another approach would be to estimate sij using Bootstrap methods [Diaconis and Efron, 1983, Efron, 1981].

objects: estimated correlation matrix; inverse correlation matrix; GLASSO
assumptions: n much smaller than p; simulated examples have sparse precision matrices
conclusion: CorShrink correlation estimates are typically nearly singular when n is much smaller than p, making their inverses unstable, whereas GLASSO is designed for sparse inverse-correlation estimation.
scope: Author-stated limitation plus bounded empirical comparison; no universal superiority claim.
span: In some applications interest may be focused on estimating the inverse of the correlation matrix, or the partial correlation matrix, rather than the correlation matrix itself. As currently implemented CorShrink is not well suited to such applications: in particular the correlation matrix estimate from CorShrink is typically close to singular when n << p, so its inverse is unstable, and does not generally provide a good estimate for the inverse-correlation matrix (in Frobenius norm, say). In contrast GLASSO is specifically designed for estimating (sparse) inverse correlation matrices, and indeed for this task GLASSO outperforms the other methods considered here on our examples (Supplementary Figure S4), which all involve sparse precision matrices.

objects: entrywise thresholding; EB sharing of information across entries
assumptions: each matrix element is treated independently in the working procedure
conclusion: CorShrink extends the Bickel-Levina and Rothman thresholding approaches by learning entrywise shrinkage through empirical Bayes information sharing.
scope: Model-based analogue of independent thresholding, with adaptive shrinkage.
span: In brief, CorShrink is a model-based extension of the approaches of Bickel and Levina [2008] and Rothman and others [2009]. Those approaches perform shrinkage using simple thresholding rules applied independently to each element of the correlation matrix. Our approach also treats each element of the matrix as independent, but uses an Empirical Bayes (EB) shrinkage approach that combines information across all elements to learn how much to shrink.

scope: Application of an earlier framework; not an asserted equivalence to its original testing problem.
span: We presented CorShrink, an application of the adaptive shrinkage framework from [Stephens, 2016] to shrinkage estimation of correlation matrices and related quantities.
